purpose: Bounded GAO-26-108703 route from working-age adults' labor attachment through Medicaid/SNAP interaction and selected-state employer concentration, preserving wages, benefit continuity, household recovery, and employer-intent gaps.

events.geography: United States national Census estimates for 2024 plus selected data from 15 state agencies across 11 states through September 2025
events.date_precision: GAO report reissued August 24, 2026; national estimates reference 2024 and selected employer data reference September 2025
events.denominator: About 28 million Medicaid-enrolled adults ages 19–64 and about 20 million adults ages 19–64 living in SNAP-receiving households; employer component is a separate selected-state universe
events.method: GAO analysis of Census labor characteristics and selected state administrative employer data; national program estimates and employer analysis are not pooled
events.missingness: Wages, hours volatility, schedule predictability, employer health coverage, benefit amount, eligibility churn, household composition, worker choice, remedy, trust, action, and exit are not retained
events.exposure: About 13.8 million Medicaid-enrolled adults and 10.6 million adults in SNAP-receiving households worked at some point in 2024; about 88% of working adults in each reported private-sector employment
events.alternatives_before_action: Alternative jobs, employer benefits, public-program alternatives, informal support, savings, and household work/care choices are not observed for the same adult
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: Medicaid and SNAP can protect medical or food budgets while work is attached to the household; working at some point does not establish adequate or stable income
events.choice_or_response: Working adults in both program-related groups were less likely than comparison wage earners to work full-time hours for 50 or more weeks per year; selected-state data identify 46 companies appearing among top employers in at least two states
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Households, employers, and public programs jointly shape the observed environment, but the report does not assign control over eligibility, wages, schedules, or employer benefit policy
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: Program enrollment and public benefit receipt are observed as institutional protection surfaces; no same-worker correction, continuity remedy, or employer response is verified
events.immediate_outcome: The report establishes work and public-benefit participation as coexisting parts of one labor and household-security system, with selected employer concentration
events.protected_outcome: Public benefits may protect food or health-cost capacity and make work or household continuity possible, but protected household security is not measured
events.sacrificed_outcome: Short annual attachment, low hours, or benefit uncertainty may expose households to insecurity, but the report does not observe individual sacrifice or reason
events.cost_risk_transfer: The report does not establish whether wages, employer benefits, medical costs, food needs, or public resources are shifted between firms, workers, households, and government
events.later_outcome: No same-person job retention, benefit churn, food or health outcome, mobility, complaint, political response, or exit is observed
events.meaning_and_attribution: Work-plus-benefit participation can be interpreted as support, constraint, or ordinary household management; blame, fairness, and employer attribution are not measured
events.public_or_collective_response: The report supplies a policy and employer-concentration signal, not worker organizing, complaint, bargaining, voting, or collective action
events.counterexample: Program use does not imply nonwork or employer wrongdoing; large employers may appear because of workforce size, sector, occupation, or place composition
events.source_and_uncertainty: GAO national Census estimates and selected-state administrative analysis; universes differ, state definitions vary, and the report was reissued with Rhode Island corrections

arrows.to: Medicaid enrollment or SNAP-receiving household status
arrows.evidence: GAO reports about 13.8 million Medicaid-enrolled adults and 10.6 million adults living in SNAP-receiving households worked at some point in 2024
arrows.counterexample: Work and program status can be jointly shaped by health, household composition, wages, hours, and eligibility; the result is coexistence, not a causal employment-to-benefit path
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-person job, eligibility, benefit amount, household need, and timing record

arrows.to: annual labor attachment and household security
arrows.evidence: Working adults connected to Medicaid or SNAP were less likely than comparison wage earners to work full-time hours for 50 or more weeks per year; the report does not measure security directly
arrows.counterexample: Shorter attachment can reflect schooling, care, disability, health, preference, or labor demand rather than benefit dependence
arrows.remaining_gap: Wages, schedule, household food/health security, churn, medical costs, and worker choice

arrows.evidence: Selected data from 15 agencies across 11 states identify 46 companies among the top 25 employers of Medicaid enrollees or SNAP beneficiaries in at least two states
arrows.counterexample: Top-employer overlap can reflect firm size, sector, occupation, or place and does not establish deliberate benefit shifting or per-worker incidence
arrows.remaining_gap: Comparable wages, hours, employer benefits, turnover, eligibility transitions, and employer policy

arrows.to: durable household security, health continuity, food security, or mobility
arrows.evidence: The GAO report identifies program and labor attachment scales but contains no same-person follow-up on benefit continuity, material outcome, or mobility
arrows.counterexample: Program receipt can buffer a household while administrative churn or low hours still leaves security fragile
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-household benefit amount, notice, effort, churn, health/food outcome, work retention, and recovery

arrows.to: employer response, worker voice, trust, political action, or exit
arrows.evidence: The selected-state employer signal does not observe firm intent, worker bargaining, complaint, policy response, institutional trust, or exit
arrows.counterexample: A concentrated employer can coexist with adequate compensation, worker preference, public support, or high mobility; concentration alone is not exploitation
arrows.remaining_gap: State-year worker-employer episode with benefits, alternatives, voice, response, household outcome, trust, and movement

boundary: This ledger formalizes work and public-benefit coexistence plus a selected-state employer-concentration signal. It does not establish employer intent, benefit shifting, causal program effects, household recovery, worker power, political response, or exit.
storage_boundary: Only GAO-published aggregate figures, universes, revision metadata, and interpretation limits are retained; Census microdata and state administrative files are not stored.
